1.title: Know computers and the service job
1.intro: Computer services keep devices and networks working for people and small firms. Start by learning the parts and the words.
pts: Name the parts: processor, memory, storage, screen, network card, power.
Describe the difference between hardware, software and a network.
Explain what a service ticket is and why every job gets one.
List words: backup, update, password, router, malware.
Compare a hard drive and a solid-state drive by speed and cost in plain words.
Explain what an operating system does.
Describe the path of a keystroke to the screen in four steps.
1.ex: A laptop is slow. The ticket says: user, device, problem, date, steps taken, result. A 500 GB disk was 98% full (490 GB used); after moving 185 GB of old files to an external drive, 305 GB are used, which is 61%.
1.act: Open a spare computer or use a parts chart. Label eight parts and say what each does.
1.std: Task: name computer parts. Condition: from a real or pictured device. Standard: eight parts named with one job each.

2.title: Find faults step by step
2.intro: Good technicians do not guess. They ask, test one thing at a time and write down the result.
pts: Apply a fault method: ask what changed, reproduce, test one thing, record.
Check the simple things first: power, cable, restart, free space, updates.
Compare two possible causes and test the cheaper one first.
Explain why you copy the user's files before you change anything.
Record the exact error message before changing anything.
Test with a second cable, port or user account to narrow the cause.
Decide when to stop and refer: burning smell, swollen battery or water damage.
2.ex: No internet on one laptop. Other devices work, so the router is fine. Wi-Fi was switched off on the laptop. Fixed in one minute; ticket updated. When two causes are possible, test the cheaper one first: a 5-minute cable swap before a 60-minute reinstall.
2.act: Fix three practice faults on a test machine and write the steps for each.
2.std: Task: find a fault. Condition: practice machine. Standard: one change at a time with the result written after each.

3.title: Follow the rules in Canada
3.intro: Technicians handle private data, so laws about privacy, licences and electronic waste matter. Check with the local authority.
pts: Explain that federal and provincial privacy laws limit how personal data is collected and used; check which applies to your clients.
Describe software licence rules: do not install unlicensed software.
Check local rules for electronic waste; many provinces have recycling programs.
Apply the rule that you do not look at private files unless the job needs it and the owner agrees.
Ask the provincial e-waste program where drives and batteries go and write the drop-off address.
Choose a drive-wipe method and get written approval before a drive leaves the client's hands.
Check which privacy law applies when you handle staff records: federal or provincial.
3.ex: Rules table row: Personal data | privacy regulator | collect only what the job needs | every job | signed consent kept. If a drive holds staff records, open only the files the job needs and note which ones.
3.act: Make a rules table for your province covering privacy, licensing and e-waste, with official pages.
3.std: Task: map the rules. Condition: official pages only. Standard: each row has an enforcer, an action and a checked date.

4.title: Set up and fix devices and networks
4.intro: Now do real set-up work to a written method.
pts: Build a new device set-up checklist: updates, user accounts, backup, security, printer, Wi-Fi.
Apply a home or office network plan: router, strong Wi-Fi password, guest network.
Install and test backups, including one restore test.
Record every setting you change so you can undo it.
Compare wired and wireless connections for an office by speed and reliability.
Test the signal in three rooms and move the router to improve the weakest one.
Draw a network map showing devices and label the cables.
4.ex: Set-up checklist for a new office laptop: update, create user, turn on disk encryption, install approved software, set backup, test restore, give password rules to the user. Planned time: 30 + 10 + 20 + 20 + 10 = 90 minutes for updates, accounts, backup, restore test and handover.
4.act: Set up a test computer and a test Wi-Fi network from the checklist and do one backup restore.
4.std: Task: set up a device. Condition: written checklist. Standard: every item ticked and a restore test passed.

5.title: Security and data safety
5.intro: Most problems come from weak sign-in, old software and phishing. Fix these first.
pts: Apply strong passwords, a password manager and two-step sign-in.
Check for phishing: odd sender, rush, link that does not match.
Explain least access: each user gets only what they need.
Create a breach plan: who is told, what is switched off, when.
Apply automatic updates and check that they actually ran.
Restore one file from backup once a month to prove it works.
Teach three staff how to report a suspicious email.
5.ex: An email says the bank account is locked with a link. The sender address is odd and the link points elsewhere. The staff member reports it and does not click. In a quiz of 5 emails, 3 phishing and 2 real, finding 4 of 5 is 80%.
5.act: Run a 20-minute safety talk for three people and a phishing quiz of five examples.
5.std: Task: improve client security. Condition: small office or home. Standard: two-step sign-in on key accounts and a written breach plan.

6.title: Price your work and plan your time
6.intro: Technicians often under-price. Count travel, waiting and learning time.
pts: Compute your hourly cost: tools, insurance, vehicle, software, unpaid time.
Compare fee types: per hour, per job, monthly support plan.
Build a day plan with travel and a buffer for jobs that run long.
Evaluate which jobs pay well and which waste time.
Calculate the hourly rate as yearly costs plus wanted income divided by billable hours.
Compare a monthly support plan with per-job pricing for a client who calls often.
Calculate unbilled time: travel, quotes and notes.
6.ex: Price 85 per hour, direct cost 10. Margin 75 per hour. If fixed costs are 1,200 a month, break-even is 1,200 / 75 = 16 hours. A 2-hour job with 1 unpaid hour of travel earns 2 x 75 = 150 over 3 hours, or 50 per hour. Teaching numbers only.
6.act: Build a cost sheet and a price list for five common jobs.
6.std: Task: price jobs. Condition: all costs counted. Standard: break-even hours correct and shown with units.

7.title: Serve clients and keep records
7.intro: Clients return when you explain clearly, keep promises and leave good notes.
pts: Explain faults in plain words, without blame or jargon.
Write a job report: problem, work done, parts, cost, advice.
Apply a follow-up check three days after each job to confirm the fix still works.
Handle a complaint: listen, restate, fix or refund as agreed.
Write next-step advice in three lines the client can follow.
Keep a log of repeat faults per client to find a deeper cause.
Identify the repeat faults from the pilot jobs and write one lasting fix for each.
7.ex: Job report: Printer would not connect. Cause: new Wi-Fi password. Work: re-connected, tested a print. Advice: write the new password in the office safe. Cost: one hour. A follow-up call on day 3 confirms it still works.
7.act: Write five job reports from practice jobs and call a practice client for a follow-up.
7.std: Task: finish a job properly. Condition: practice job. Standard: client can read the report and knows what to do next.

8.title: Run the service for real
8.intro: Now run your service with real clients, support plans and a growth plan.
pts: Run a 60-day pilot with at least five clients or a volunteer help desk.
Review weekly: jobs, time per job, repeats, client feedback.
Create a 12-month plan with training goals and tools budget.
Lead others: write the checklists so a helper can repeat your standard.
Calculate average time per job and hours paid at the end of the pilot.
Compare client feedback with the stop rule.
Create a checklist for a helper and test it on one job.
8.ex: Stop rule: if fewer than 20 paid hours in 60 days, stop and write lessons. Result: 34 hours x 75 = 2,550 in margin, minus 2,400 fixed costs for two months = 150, and two monthly support clients; add a second service.
8.act: Run the pilot, write the review and present your plan to three people.
8.std: Task: run a computer service pilot. Condition: 60 days, real clients. Standard: results compared with the stop rule and privacy rules re-checked.

quiz: What is a service ticket?
A written record of the user, device, problem, steps and result.
Why test one thing at a time?
So you know which change fixed or caused the problem.
Why copy files before a repair?
To avoid losing the user's data.
What do you do about unlicensed software?
Do not install it.
Which law area covers personal data?
Privacy laws, federal and provincial; check which applies.
What are signs of phishing?
Odd sender, rush, and a link that does not match.
Why do a restore test?
A backup is only proven when you can restore from it.
What is least access?
Each user gets only the access they need.
How do you find break-even hours?
Fixed cost divided by margin per hour.
What goes in a job report?
Problem, work done, parts, cost and advice.
